title: Runtime LTS (Private Deployments) — Enterprise Requirements Intake (Sales/CS)
content:
Sheet purpose
- This is a running intake of enterprise requirements gathered via Sales, Solutions, Support/CS, and deal desks specifically for Runtime LTS in Private/VPC/on-prem deployments.
- Intended to feed: Enterprise Runtime LTS PRD, Private installer work (pin/pull/rollback), change-management process, and customer-facing release note format.

Last update summary (2025-12-05)
- Repeated theme: customers will accept slower feature velocity if they get predictable patch cadence + clean, risk-scored release notes + evidence they can hand to auditors.
- Notification expectations are stricter for Private than Hosted (some customers require 10+ business days lead time for upgrades, even for “recommended” patches).
- “Support window” questions are coming up in deals; need a crisp statement about how long a given LTS line is supported and what “support” means (patches vs. troubleshooting vs. hotfixes).

Assumptions / definitions (working)
- “Private” includes VPC and on-prem packages installed/operated by customer teams, with Redwood support.
- “Runtime LTS line” example: runtime-1.20-lts (patches: 1.20-lts.0, 1.20-lts.1, ...)
- “Patch” means bug/security/perf regression fixes only (no behavior changes unless explicitly called out as breaking/mitigation required).
- “Emergency patch” means out-of-band patch cadence (security or severe correctness); subject to accelerated comms + explicit customer opt-in for install window.


TAB 1 — Summary of requirements (normalized)
(Each requirement is phrased as what the enterprise expects; notes include where we heard it most often.)

1) Upgrade windows + operational cadence
- Requirement: Customer can choose an install window (e.g., Sat 02:00–06:00 local) and avoid mid-week surprises.
- Requirement: Standard patch cadence that is predictable (e.g., every 2–4 weeks) + a published “next patch ETA” even if tentative.
- Requirement: No forced upgrades for Private deployments; Redwood can recommend but not auto-apply.
- Requirement: Upgrade path must be supported for N-1 patch versions within a line (e.g., 1.20-lts.0 → 1.20-lts.3 is supported).
- Requirement: Clear statement about cross-line upgrades (e.g., 1.20-lts → 1.22-lts) including compatibility risks and required installer versions.
Notes: Strongest in regulated industries (finance/healthcare) and customers with formal change advisory boards.

2) Rollback expectations
- Requirement: Rollback procedure is documented, tested, and does not require “state surgery” (no manual KV cache/persistent storage edits).
- Requirement: Rollback must be possible to immediate prior patch version within the same LTS line.
- Requirement: If rollback is blocked by data format change, that must be explicitly stated as “Rollback Constraint” in release notes with mitigation.
- Requirement: Redwood provides a validation checklist (smoke tests + perf sanity checks) post-upgrade and post-rollback.
Notes: Rollback concerns are higher for scheduler changes and kernel/quantization changes.

3) Release notes quality (“slower-change notes”)
- Requirement: Release notes must be short, operationally oriented, and include a risk level.
- Requirement: Explicitly say “What changed / Why it matters / Who is impacted / Known issues / Mitigations / How to roll back”.
- Requirement: Separate “Customer-facing changes” from “Internal refactors/noise”; customers do not want to scan dozens of internal PRs.
- Requirement: Include perf deltas (at least a headline: p95 latency delta and throughput delta vs previous LTS patch) for a standard benchmark set.
- Requirement: Explicit “No behavior change expected” statement when true.
Notes: Support tickets cite current runtime notes as too verbose and too engineering-centric.

4) Audit and compliance evidence
- Requirement: Provide artifact provenance (signatures/hashes) and a trace from issue → PR → build attestation → released artifact.
- Requirement: Provide a release evidence bundle on request (PDF or zipped export) containing approvals, CI results, benchmark summary, SBOM (if available), and artifact digests.
- Requirement: For security patches, include CVE mapping and whether it’s remotely exploitable, plus recommended timeline.
- Requirement: Evidence retention: customers want at least 12–24 months available, even after an LTS line exits support.
Notes: Several accounts explicitly asked for “audit-ready paperwork” rather than “trust us, tests passed”.

5) Support expectations (Private + Enterprise)
- Requirement: Stated response times for LTS patch incidents (e.g., Sev1 initial response within 1 hour for Premium support).
- Requirement: Clear escalation path for “need backport” requests; customers want to know decision time and what info to provide.
- Requirement: A policy on “customer-specific hotfixes” (generally avoided) vs. “emergency LTS patch” (preferred).
- Requirement: One named release contact for LTS patches (release manager alias) + a support alias.
Notes: Especially common in larger enterprises who’ve had “support ping-pong” on runtime regressions.

6) Compatibility guarantees
- Requirement: Compatibility statement for Private installer versions (minimum supported installer for each LTS line).
- Requirement: Kubernetes version support matrix for Private (EKS/GKE/AKS and on-prem distros) with LTS runtime.
- Requirement: GPU driver/CUDA compatibility statement and “known good” combos.
- Requirement: Model compatibility statement (what model families are supported/verified for LTS) and explicit exclusions.
Notes: Customers treat Private as “platform” and want stability across adjacent dependencies.

7) Notifications + comms cadence
- Requirement: Notification at least 5–10 business days before a standard patch is “recommended” (some accounts want 14 days).
- Requirement: Emergency patches: immediate notification with severity + recommended timeframe + mitigation if can’t patch.
- Requirement: A single place to subscribe (email list + optional webhook) with consistent subject lines.
- Requirement: Patch announcements must include: version, risk level, summary, CVEs (if any), upgrade steps, rollback steps, and evidence availability.
Notes: Comms expectations differ by account; need a baseline policy + per-account override.


TAB 2 — Account/deal signals (anonymized; sourced from HubSpot/SUP tickets)
(Use for prioritization; not all details are shared outside Product/CS. Keep customer names out of general circulation.)

Columns: Account/Deal | Deployment | Driver | Requested support window | Patch cadence ask | Notification ask | Audit ask | Top pain | Notes / source

1) Deal 118203 | Private (VPC) | Close requirement | 18 months | Monthly preferred | 10 biz days standard; 48h emergency | Provenance + evidence bundle | Upgrade churn every minor runtime | Source: hubspot:deal_118203 + gmail:2025-11-19 thread
2) Account 55291 | Private (on-prem) | Stability | 24 months | Every 4–6 weeks | 14 biz days standard | Strong (SOC2/ISO-aligned) | CAB approvals, slow install windows | Source: hubspot:account_55291 + SUP-3921
3) SUP-3950 (existing enterprise) | Dedicated + Private hybrid | Regression avoidance | 12–18 months | Monthly | 7 biz days | Medium | Perf regression after minor upgrade | Wants backport instead of upgrade; source: jira:SUP-3950
4) SUP-3988 (existing enterprise) | Private (VPC) | Release note clarity | N/A | N/A | N/A | Low | Notes too noisy; wants risk level | Source: jira:SUP-3988


TAB 3 — “Must-have” vs “Nice-to-have” (Product cut line)
Must-have (to pilot LTS with enterprise Private)
- Published support window per LTS line + definition of what’s supported
- Patch cadence + emergency patch policy
- Private installer can pin/pull LTS artifacts and supports rollback to prior patch
- Enterprise-style release notes template (risk level, known issues, mitigations)
- Provenance: artifact digests + signing/attestation (at least for runtime images)
- Backport request intake + decision SLA (even if manual at first)

Nice-to-have (often requested; may be phased)
- Customer self-serve portal for evidence bundles
- Automated webhook notifications (Slack/MS Teams) per account
- SBOM published for each patch
- Pre-upgrade “compatibility scanner” (cluster/GPU/driver validation)


TAB 4 — Proposed baseline policy knobs (for review)
(These are not final commitments; capturing what we likely need to standardize.)

1) Support window (proposal)
- Baseline: 12 months of patch support per LTS line; target 18 months for enterprise contracts requiring it (deal-dependent).
- Evidence retention: 24 months minimum for artifacts + release evidence availability.

2) Patch cadence (proposal)
- Standard: every 4 weeks (target), with ability to skip if no eligible fixes (publish “no-op month” note).
- Emergency: as needed; run accelerated gates + canary; comms within same business day.

3) Notification baseline (proposal)
- Standard: 7 business days notice before marking a patch “Recommended for Private”.
- Emergency: immediate email + follow-up guidance; provide mitigation if patch must be deferred.

4) Risk levels (proposal)
- Low: config/docs, non-invasive correctness fixes, no perf risk expected.
- Medium: scheduler adjustments, kernel changes with limited surface, perf improvement or targeted regression fix.
- High: changes touching batching/cache semantics, memory management, multi-GPU scheduling, or known conflict areas.


Open questions / follow-ups
- What do we want to promise as the default support window without creating an unbounded backport tail? (Need alignment with Runtime + Release Eng.)
- How do we handle “security fix on mainline requires dependency bump” when LTS forbids churn? (Need Security/Compliance input.)
- What’s the minimum acceptable provenance story for enterprise audits in Phase 1? (Marcus Lin + Olga Petrov to advise.)
- How do we define and publish the compatibility matrix (K8s, drivers, CUDA) without over-committing? (Private + SRE.)

Next steps (owner → due)
- Vivek Kulkarni: convert Must-haves into PRD acceptance criteria + tie to PM-813 rollout plan → 2025-12-12
- Connor O'Brien / Sahana Iyer: confirm what evidence/signing we can ship for pilot LTS patches → 2025-12-13
- Kira Thompson: draft Private upgrade + rollback one-pager aligned to LTS versioning language → 2025-12-16
- Dev Patel: propose Support intake form + decision SLA for backport requests (incl. required logs, repro) → 2025-12-18

Notes / raw quotes (verbatim-ish from calls/tickets; anonymized)
- “We can’t upgrade every time there’s a minor release; we need a stable line and backports.”
- “Our auditors want hashes and a chain of custody. A screenshot of CI isn’t enough.”
- “If you tell us it’s low risk and give us a rollback plan, we can schedule it. If not, it sits for months.”
- “Please stop listing every internal refactor in release notes; just tell us what’s different operationally.”
